- When sentiment is consistently low or neutral (≤0.17) over recent days, model tends to underpredict; adjust forecast upward slightly to avoid underreaction.
- After a sharp price spike (e.g., >+5% from prior day), model often overreacts and forecasts too high; cap forecast at +3–5% above recent peak to avoid overshoot.
- If true outcome shows strong mean reversion (e.g., 3–5 consecutive days of downward drift), model often fails to recognize it; reduce forecast slope or add slight downward bias.
- When sentiment turns positive (e.g., >0.17) after a dip, model frequently overcorrects; dampen forecast rise by 10–20% to avoid overbought bias.
- For 30-day horizon, model often overestimates volatility in early days; apply smoothing or decay factor to reduce early forecast magnitude.
- If sentiment history shows repeated negative sentiment (e.g., 3+ days of 0.00), model tends to ignore downward pressure; add a 0.5–1.0 point downward bias to forecast.
- When true outcome is significantly below model (e.g., >2% gap), check if sentiment was negative — if so, model may be “too optimistic”; reduce forecast by 0.5–1.5 points to align with sentiment.
- If model forecast is consistently above true outcome by >1.5 points over 3–5 days, consider sentiment-driven mean reversion — reduce forecast by 0.3–0.7 points per day to reflect sentiment decay.
